name: Yuzu extract

lead: Yuzu is a tart citrus fruit grown mainly in Japan and Korea, and extracts of its peel, juice or seed appear in some Asian skin-care products for their vitamin C and polyphenol content. People use it for brighter, more even skin tone.

The chain is antioxidant and pigment: in cell studies a yuzu seed compound, nomilin, showed antioxidant activity and lowered melanin production in cultured melanoma cells, pointing to less pigment and a more even tone. Published work is laboratory and animal studies; human skin trials were not found.

paras: Used in serums, creams, masks and toners as a brightening step, typically in a morning and evening routine paired with sunscreen, which tone-evening depends on. Users generally look for changes over several weeks.
No specific safety data for cosmetic use were found; citrus ingredients can irritate or sensitise some skin. A patch test is the usual precaution.

angle.text: Yuzu extract is used in Asian skincare as a vitamin C and polyphenol botanical for brighter, more even skin tone. A yuzu seed compound showed antioxidant activity and lowered melanin production in cell studies, which is the route to less pigment.

lead: Yuzu (Citrus junos) is a tart, aromatic citrus fruit believed to have originated in central China and now grown mainly in Japan and Korea.[1] Extracts of the peel, juice or seed appear in some Asian skin-care products, usually marketed for their vitamin C and polyphenol content.[2]

Published work on yuzu extract consists mostly of laboratory and animal studies on antioxidant, antiplatelet and pigment-related activity. No human trial of yuzu extract for skin appearance was found.
infobox: Central China; grown in Japan, Korea

paras: Wikipedia describes yuzu as resembling a small yellow mandarin, used in Japan and Korea in condiments, teas and preserves, with peel oil marketed as a fragrance.[1] A Japanese custom, the winter-solstice yuzu bath, floats whole fruits in hot water and is said to soften skin and relax the mind.[1]

A 2022 study reported that nomilin from yuzu seed had antioxidant activity and reduced melanin production in cultured mouse melanoma cells through the PKA/CREB pathway; the authors describe yuzu peel and seed as rich in vitamin C, citric acid and polyphenols.[2] Other studies examined methanolic and ethanolic yuzu extracts, and hesperidin and naringin, finding inhibition of platelet aggregation in rat and human blood samples.[3][4] A rat study found that long-term oral yuzu extract reduced cognitive decline in a beta-amyloid model.[5]

No studies found on yuzu extract for skin. Registered human trials of citron (Citrus junos) peel extract concern blood cholesterol, and a supplement trial in perimenopausal symptoms is listed.[6][7] The pigment and antioxidant findings above come from cell and animal work.
